newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian oil safe during Kremlin health scare.
newsitem.headline: Russian oil safe during Kremlin health scare.

text.p: Executives, not the Kremlin, are the real power brokers in Russia's oil industry, so markets need not fret over fears of political instability caused by President Boris Yeltsin's health problems, oil analysts said on Friday.

"During the 1990s, our country has been ruled by military generals, oil generals and industrialists, no matter what parliament says," said Eugene Khartukov of the International Centre for Petroleum Studies in Moscow.
"One single leader is not as crucial as he used to be (in Russia)," said Elena Merkoulova, oil analyst at Salomon Brothers in London.
Western oil traders have been keeping a close eye on Yeltsin's health since before his heart surgery last November. He has been in hospital for over a week with pneumonia.
Dealers appear to be adjusting to dwindling central control, but developments in Moscow still unsettle them.

"It will take a while for people to accept that this central control of everything that happens in Russia has come to an end," said Julian Leigh, analyst at the Centre for Global Energy Studies in London.

Jitters in world oil markets over political instability in Russia are understandable -- Russia is the world's third largest oil producer, exporting about a third of its daily output of 6.2 million barrels per day (bpd).

Fuel and energy ministry figures show Russian crude exports outside the Commonwealth of Independent States rose nearly five percent in the first 11 months of last year to 92.8 million tonnes, despite a five-percent drop in output to 275.9 million tonnes during the same period.
And Russian government control over deliveries has not completely vanished -- it can still influence allocations of crude oil for domestic needs.
But analysts said stormy weather at export outlets like Novorossiisk in the Black Sea was far more likely to influence crude supplies than changes in government leadership.
They said Russian oil exports to the West looked secure in the short term and deliveries could even rise were it not for constraints to the existing port and pipeline systems.
"Russian exports will depend closely on the bottlenecking of export outlets," Khartukov said.
He estimated Russia could export another 10 to 25 million tonnes a year (200,000 to 500,000 bpd) of crude by the end of the century if outlets could be found.
But the long term outlook for domestic production was less promising as companies had been slow to invest in new developments in Russia, analysts said.
"The banks see the role of oil companies to provide them with quick cash profits rather than investing in new developments and new fields," Leigh said.
The focus for Russian and Western oil companies was increasingly on projects in countries of the former Soviet Union like Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan, he added.
"This year we are looking at a small decline in Russian output, but this will be more than offset by the rise in production in Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan," Leigh said.
